nameStory: The 'moundlily' part of this yucca's name comes from its impressive flower spike that shoots up like a giant lily stem from a mounded base of sword-like leaves. 'Gloriosa' means 'glorious' in Latin, referring to the spectacular white flower clusters that can tower up to 8 feet tall. It's also called soft-tipped yucca because unlike some of its razor-sharp relatives, the leaf tips are relatively blunt and won't puncture you quite as easily!
description: Moundlily yucca is an architectural evergreen shrub that looks like it belongs in a desert but can surprisingly survive New England winters. It forms a dramatic rosette of thick, sword-shaped blue-green leaves that can grow up to 8 feet tall when it sends up its towering flower spike. The plant creates a striking focal point in any landscape with its bold, geometric form that stays green year-round. This is definitely not your typical New England native - it's a southern transplant that's tough enough to handle our climate.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, leathery sword-shaped leaves arranged in a rosette pattern, blue-green in color with relatively soft tips that won't severely puncture skin like other yuccas. The leaves feel waxy and substantial to the touch.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Spectacular white bell-shaped flowers arranged in a tall, dense spike that can reach 8 feet high. Each flower is creamy white and waxy, hanging downward like little lanterns.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a symmetrical rosette of leaves growing from a central point, creating a fountain-like or architectural appearance that stays the same shape year-round.

idTips.label: Trunk
idTips.description: May develop a short, thick trunk over time, giving it an almost palm-tree-like appearance, though many remain trunkless rosettes close to the ground.

habitat: In New England, you'll almost exclusively find moundlily yucca in cultivated settings like gardens, landscaping, and around buildings where it's been planted as an ornamental. It thrives in well-drained soils and sunny locations, often used in xeriscaping or Mediterranean-style gardens. With only one recorded observation in New England, this is definitely a rare garden escapee rather than an established wild plant.

seasonality.spring: Evergreen leaves remain blue-green and architectural. New growth may emerge from the center of the rosette as warmer weather arrives.
seasonality.summer: This is when the magic happens - the dramatic flower spike shoots up rapidly, producing masses of creamy white bell-shaped blooms that are fragrant in the evening.
seasonality.fall: Flower spike may persist with developing seed pods. Leaves remain unchanged, providing year-round structure in the landscape.
seasonality.winter: Maintains its evergreen rosette of sword-like leaves, providing bold winter interest. The thick, waxy leaves help it survive New England's harsh winters.

funFact: Yucca flowers can only be pollinated by tiny yucca moths in one of nature's most exclusive partnerships - the moths lay their eggs inside the flowers and deliberately pollinate them, ensuring their larvae will have yucca seeds to eat, but they're careful to leave enough seeds for the plant to reproduce!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with common yucca, but moundlily yucca has broader, more blue-green leaves with softer tips, while common yucca has narrower, darker green leaves with sharp, needle-like points and curly white threads along the edges.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'moundlily yucca,' this plant isn't related to true lilies at all - it's actually in the asparagus family! Many people assume all yuccas are desert plants, but several species have adapted to survive much colder climates than their southwestern cousins.
compareHints: Moundlily yucca has broader, blue-green leaves with relatively soft tips compared to common yucca's narrow, dark green leaves with sharp points and curly white threads. Weak-leaf yucca is similar but has even more flexible leaves that actually bend and curve rather than standing rigidly upright. The flower spikes of moundlily yucca also tend to be taller and more impressive than its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common yucca has the most prominent curly white fibers along its leaf edges compared to its relatives.

Weak-leaf yucca is distinguished from common yucca by its notably flexible leaves that bend rather than remaining rigid, and from moundlily yucca by its ground-hugging rosette growth habit rather than forming a trunk.
